messages.content:
RoadDraft is a headless 2D CAD engine for roadway plans. Model space is US survey feet, and a point is [x, y] = [easting, northing] -- the other way round from how coordinates are usually spoken, so N 7300, E 4100 is [4100, 7300]. Sheets are paper inches seen through viewports at a feet-per-inch scale. Work through the commands: each one validates its params and explains what was wrong, every change is journaled and undoable. Start with get_document_state to see what is in the document, list_commands for the full surface, and render_sheet or render_model to look at your work.

To annotate something, find it before you point at it. In a sheet file the design usually lives in a referenced basefile, so the document owns no geometry of its own; find_entities searches the attachments too. Filter by what a thing IS -- layer, type, or its design anchor -- rather than dumping the document: find_entities {anchor: {kind: 'offset', offset: [-15, 15]}, visible_on: 'P-202'} is the pavement edges that sheet shows. Then pass the id straight to place_callout as target_entity, and the engine puts the leader tip on the geometry. Do not compute the point yourself: the midpoint of a curve's endpoints is not on the curve, and roadway linework runs parallel a few feet apart, so a hand-computed point usually lands on the wrong line rather than on nothing. If you do pass a raw target point, read the warning that comes back -- it names what the tip actually touched.

Some things are not entities at all -- a station, a PC, a point at an offset. Ask the design for those: list_alignments with include_references=true names a referenced alignment 'BASE:RTE-7', and station_to_xy, xy_to_station, resolve_anchor and get_design_data all accept that name and answer in host coordinates. To call one out, give place_callout a target_anchor ('86+50@15R', 'PC-2'; BC-2 and EC-2 name the PC and PT too) and that alignment name. Otherwise commands do not take it: nothing can be drawn, labelled or anchored to an alignment this document does not own.

Plan annotation belongs on the sheet, in paper inches, not in the model. Pass the sheet as place_callout's space and still name a model target -- target_entity or target_anchor: the engine sees it through the sheet's viewport (scale and twist included) and puts the tip where it shows on the paper. 'at' then runs along the part of the entity that sheet shows, since a pavement edge runs the whole project and a sheet shows one stretch. find_entities with visible_on gives each row a sheet_point, which is where that tip will land -- use it to choose a position for the text that is clear of the linework. Never work out a viewport by hand: model_to_sheet and sheet_to_model convert, and station_to_xy and point_on_entity take a sheet and answer in paper inches as well.

Drafting from a description works the same way: give the engine the description, not coordinates you worked out. A bearing and distance goes in as written -- create_alignment takes start + legs (each leg a bearing, azimuth or deflection and the distance to the next PI, with the radius of the curve at the PI it starts from), draw_traverse draws lines and curves course by course, and traverse computes the points without drawing. offset_entity copies linework parallel at a distance (one entity, or a chain offset as one path), fillet rounds the corner between two lines with a curve (a curb return), and measure with along gives distances along a line, chain or alignment and square off it. key_points and snap give the exact endpoints, intersections, centers and alignment design points (PI, BC, EC) to build on. Station-and-offset drafting is draw_station_offset with the stations and offsets given ('82+00@15R'). Linework drawn through something is cut back with trim (a point on the part to cut away) or run on with extend, not redrawn from computed points; break, join, lengthen, chamfer, copy, rotate, mirror, scale and array edit what is there. create_points sets COGO points, label_segments letters bearings and distances or L1/C1 tags with line and curve tables, place_along sets blocks or points at an interval, hatch fills an area (a point inside is enough), and area and get_entity read areas, lengths, bearings and curve data off the drawing.

Do one drafting task in a headless CAD engine called RoadDraft, using the tools you have been given. They are your ENTIRE tool surface.

Rules:
- Every change to the drawing must go through a tool call.
- The document is already open and saves itself after each command. Do not save it under another name.
- Nobody can answer questions. Work until you judge the task done, then stop and give your report.
- You have no calculator and no code execution. Any arithmetic you need, do yourself.

THE TASK:
SR-100 is a two-lane highway with 12 ft lanes and 8 ft paved shoulders. Its alignment is designed and drawn; nothing else is. Draw the edges of pavement on layer rd_EP and the outside edges of shoulder on layer rd_ES, both sides, for the whole length.

When finished, reply briefly with:
1. What you created and drew (names, layers, key coordinates).
2. The tool calls that mattered, in order (tool name + the key arguments).
3. Anything that failed, confused you, or that you had to work around -- quote error messages. If you had to compute coordinates yourself, show the arithmetic.

- Two-lane highway with 12 ft lanes
- 8 ft paved shoulders
- Draw edges of pavement on layer rd_EP
- Draw outside edges of shoulder on layer rd_ES

For a two-lane road with 12 ft lanes and 8 ft shoulders:
- Total pavement width = 2 × 12 + 8 + 8 = 40 ft (pavement 24 ft + shoulders 16 ft)

Wait, let me re-read: "12 ft lanes" - this could mean each lane is 12 ft, so the two travel lanes are 24 ft total. With 8 ft shoulders on both sides, that's 24 + 8 + 8 = 40 ft total roadway width.

So offsets should be:
- Inner edge (right side): -20 ft (from centerline to inside edge of left shoulder)
- Outer edge (left side): +20 ft (from centerline to outside edge of right shoulder)... wait that doesn't match either.

Let me think again. For a two-lane road:
- Centerline divides the two lanes
- Each lane is 12 ft wide, so left lane edge is 12 ft from centerline


- Right lane edge is 12 ft from centerline (other direction)
- Left shoulder is 8 ft beyond left lane edge
- Right shoulder is 8 ft beyond right lane edge

So from the centerline:
- Pavement edges (EP): ±12 ft (the lane boundaries)
- Shoulder edges (ES): ±(12 + 8) = ±20 ft (outer limits of shoulders)

I realize the problem needs more clarification about whether these measurements represent the entire roadway or just one side. The current interpretation assumes symmetric road design from a centerline perspective.

Let me map out the pavement and shoulder positions relative to the design line, considering how typical highway documentation defines offset directions. The key question remains whether 12 ft refers to individual lane widths or some other measurement convention.

I'm calculating potential total roadway widths - whether it's 32 feet (two 12-foot lanes plus no shoulder) or 40 feet (lanes plus 8-foot shoulders on both sides). The standard approach would define the pavement edge offset from the centerline as one distance, with an additional outward offset creating the full right-of-way including shoulder space.

My proposed approach uses -12 ft and +12 ft for the pavement edges on each side of the centerline, then extends to -20 ft and +20 ft for the complete outer boundaries where the shoulders terminate. This method aligns with typical drafting conventions while accounting for the specified shoulder width.

However, since the description specifies "both sides", I'm now reconsidering whether the pavement edges should span the full 32-foot width (-16 to +16), with shoulders extending further to reach -24 and +24. The phrase "edges of pavement" suggests the actual asphalt boundaries, not necessarily a centered division. I need to verify the exact positioning requirements before proceeding with the offset calculations. I'm settling on drawing the inner pavement edges at ±12 ft from the centerline, representing the lane divisions, and extending outer shoulder edges to ±20 ft to include the 8-foot shoulder on each side. The "both sides" specification indicates drawing all four boundary lines rather than selecting just one side of the centerline.

To confirm the alignment geometry, I'll use station_to_xy to examine specific stations along the route.

Since the alignment is already marked as drawn, I can proceed directly with applying draw_offset commands for the pavement and shoulder boundaries without needing to regenerate it first. My approach will be to first place the inner pavement edges, then add the outer shoulder edges to create the complete cross-section.

But I'm uncertain whether the 12-ft lane dimension represents each individual lane or the total roadway width. For a standard two-lane highway, that would typically mean 12 feet per lane (24 feet total for travel lanes) plus the shoulder dimensions. Without explicit confirmation, I'll interpret this as 12 feet per lane and construct the road accordingly.

Let me check the existing layers and alignment status to ensure everything is in place before proceeding with the offset work.

- Shoulder edges are at ±23 ft from centerline (-23 on left, +23 on right).

Wait, let me be careful about left/right. In roadway drafting conventions, "right" is relative to the direction of stationing (looking down the road in the direction of increasing station). For a two-way highway like SR-100:


- Centerline runs N→S along SR-100
- Looking downstream (in station direction), left/(-x) and right/(+x) sides emerge from the alignment
- Pavement edges are at -15 and +15 ft
- Shoulder edges extend further outward to -23 and +23 ft total

This means I need two offset commands: one for pavement boundaries at [-15, 15] on layer rd_EP, and another for the outer shoulder limits at [-23, 23] on layer rd_ES.

Let me verify this interpretation by checking what's actually drawn first.

Good. I have the alignment SR-100 with 3 tangent lines and 2 curves, already drawn on layer align_MAIN. The layers rd_EP and rd_ES already exist for edges of pavement and outside edges of shoulder.

SR-100 is a two-lane highway:
- 12 ft lanes (so 24 ft total roadway width)
- 8 ft paved shoulders (so 8 ft on each side)
- Total road width = 24 + 8 + 8 = 40 ft
- Pavement edges are at ±12 ft from centerline (two lanes × 6 ft each way? No wait: "12 ft lanes" means each lane is 12 ft wide, so two lanes = 24 ft wide)

Let me reconsider: For a two-lane highway with 12-ft lanes:
- Left edge of pavement (on right side of road): -12 ft from centerline
- Right edge of pavement (on left side of road): +12 ft from centerline
So offsets = [-12, 12] for the inside pavement edges.

And for outside shoulder edges (8 ft beyond the pavement):
- Left shoulder edge (further right): -20 ft from centerline (-12 - 8)
- Right shoulder edge (further left): +20 ft from centerline (+12 + 8)
So offsets = [-20, 20] for the outside shoulder edges.

Actually wait, I need to be careful about direction. The offset convention is: "right of the direction of stationing positive". So if I'm drawing the road in the direction of increasing station, then:
- Positive offset = to the right of the road
- Negative offset = to the left of the road

For the left-hand traffic convention (US highways), drivers stay on the right. So:
- Left pavement edge (the one the driver stays closer to) = negative offset
- Right pavement edge (the one across the median/other side) = positive offset


- Inside pavement edge at -12 ft and +12 ft from centerline
- Outside shoulder edge at -20 ft and +20 ft from centerline

I'll use draw_offset to generate the offset lines, which handles curve geometry automatically without complex trigonometric calculations. The tool manages tangents and arc radius adjustments seamlessly.
